passages.t: Seen with their own eyes, and not yet understood
passages.happening:
The third address of Moses begins. “These are the words of the covenant that the LORD commanded Moses to make with the Israelites in the land of Moab, in addition to the covenant He had made with them at Horeb” (verse 1).

Moses calls all Israel together and reminds them of what they have seen: what God did in Egypt, ‘the great trials, and those miraculous signs and wonders’ (verses 2-3).

Then he says something hard. “Yet to this day the LORD has not given you a mind to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear” (verse 4).

He goes on with the story. For forty years in the wilderness their clothes and sandals did not wear out (verse 5). They defeated Sihon and Og and took their land (verses 7-8). “So keep and follow the words of this covenant, that you may prosper in all you do” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The covenant made at Horeb is now renewed in Moab, with the children of those who first received it. It is not a different covenant. It is the same bond, taken up by a new generation at the edge of the land.

Like the treaties of that world, the speech begins with history. Before the people are asked to commit themselves, they are reminded of what God has already done for them.

Verse 4 is the surprise. These people have seen more of God's power than any people in history, and Moses says they still do not understand. Seeing a miracle is one thing. Having a heart that grasps what it means is another. In Hebrew thought the heart is where a person thinks, decides and stays loyal. Moses says that such a heart is something God gives, and that they do not yet have it.

This is not said to crush them. It is an honest statement of their need, placed at the start of the covenant. It prepares for the promise in the next chapter, where God says he will change the heart himself (30:6).

Verse 6 gives the purpose of the wilderness years. They had no ordinary bread or wine. They lived on what God provided day by day, ‘so that you might know that I am the LORD your God’.

The hard question below takes up verse 4.
passages.later:
Jesus asked his own disciples the question of verse 4, after they had seen him feed thousands: ‘Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear?’ (Mark 8:18).

Paul quotes this verse in his long discussion of why many of his own people had not believed the message about Jesus (Romans 11:8). In the same chapter he insists that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). The note on Romans 11 sets out his argument.

The prophet Ezekiel carried God's answer to verse 4: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).
passages.hard:
If God had not given Israel a heart to understand, how could Israel be blamed for not obeying?

Verse 4 says plainly that God had not yet given Israel a mind to understand. The chapter goes on to hold Israel responsible for turning away. The question of how God's rule and human responsibility fit together runs through the whole Bible, and Christian traditions answer it differently.

Reformed interpreters tend to read the verse as showing that spiritual understanding is God's gift. He gives it freely and is not obliged to give it, and people remain responsible for the sin that comes from their own hearts.

Wesleyan and Arminian interpreters tend to read it as describing Israel's lasting hardness, which God has not yet overcome because they have resisted him. On this reading it is not a decree that made obedience impossible.

Many readers of every tradition note that the verse works as a confession of need. It looks ahead to 30:6, where God promises to circumcise their hearts so that they will love him.

The chapter holds both truths and does not explain how they fit. These notes take no side. The chapter's own last verse may be its comment: some things belong to God, and what he has made known is given to be obeyed.
passages.asks: Israel had seen everything and still did not understand. Ask what you have seen of God's goodness that has not yet changed how you live. And notice that understanding is called a gift. Ask God for a heart that grasps what your eyes have already seen.

passages.happening:
Moses looks at the crowd and names who is there. “All of you are standing today before the LORD your God”: the leaders of the tribes, the elders, the officials, all the men, the children and the wives, ‘and the foreigners in your camps who cut your wood and draw your water’ (verses 10-11).

They stand there to enter the covenant and its oath, so that God ‘may establish you today as His people, and He may be your God as He promised you and as He swore to your fathers, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob’ (verse 13).

And the covenant reaches further than the crowd. “I am making this covenant and this oath not only with you, but also with those who are standing here with us today in the presence of the LORD our God, as well as with those who are not here today” (verses 14-15).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world a covenant was made in public. All the parties stood before witnesses and swore.

The list in verses 10 and 11 goes from the top of Israel to the bottom. It starts with the heads of the tribes. It ends with the foreigners who cut wood and carry water, the lowest workers in the camp. Women and children are named. No one is too small to be included, and no one is too great to be bound.

The word ‘today’ comes again and again. The covenant is not a memory. It is being made now, with the people who are present.

Then verse 15 opens it to those who are absent. ‘Those who are not here today’ means the generations still to be born. In Israel's understanding a child born later was already a party to the covenant of the ancestors. Each generation would stand where this one stood.

The heart of the covenant is the pair of promises in verse 13: you will be his people, and he will be your God. It rests on what God swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob long before anyone in the crowd was born. They are entering something far older than themselves.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua tells of a people of Canaan, the Gibeonites, who came under Israel's protection and were made ‘woodcutters and water carriers for the whole congregation’ (Joshua 9:21).

On the day of Pentecost Peter spoke of God's promise in the pattern of verse 15: “This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off” (Acts 2:39).

At his last meal Jesus took a cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you” (Luke 22:20).
passages.asks: The water carriers stood in the same line as the chiefs. Ask whether, in your church or community, the least regarded people are counted as fully as the leaders. And think of those not yet born. Ask what you are handing on to people who will come after you and whom you will never meet.

passages.t: A bitter root, and a ruined land
passages.happening:
Moses warns of a danger inside the people. They have seen the idols of Egypt and of the nations on the road (verses 16-17). “Make sure there is no man or woman, clan or tribe among you today whose heart turns away from the LORD our God to go and worship the gods of those nations. Make sure there is no root among you that bears such poisonous and bitter fruit” (verse 18).

He describes such a person. Hearing the oath, he ‘invokes a blessing on himself, saying, “I will have peace, even though I walk in the stubbornness of my own heart”’ (verse 19). Moses says that God's anger will burn against that man, and that every curse in the book will fall on him (verses 20-21).

Then he pictures a later day. The land lies burned and barren, like Sodom and Gomorrah (verse 23). The nations ask, ‘Why has the LORD done such a thing to this land?’ (verse 24). The answer is given: ‘It is because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The picture of the root is carefully chosen. A root is out of sight, and it starts small. One person's turning away, kept private, grows into something that poisons many. The plant named in the Hebrew was known for its bitterness.

The man of verse 19 has a particular kind of false comfort. He belongs to the covenant people. He has heard the oath with everyone else. And he tells himself that belonging will keep him safe while he does as he likes. He treats the covenant as a charm. Moses says that this attitude will find no forgiveness. It is not looking for any. The words are aimed at settled, self-assured defiance. They are not aimed at a person who has sinned and is afraid.

The later scene, in verses 22 to 28, is told as a conversation. Foreigners and later generations look at the ruined land and ask why. The answer does not blame God's weakness or the strength of an enemy. It names the broken covenant.

Readers date these verses in different ways. Those who think Deuteronomy was written late see in them the exile to Babylon, after 587 or 586 BC. Those who hold that the words come from Moses read them as spoken beforehand. On either view Israel's own Scripture explains Israel's disaster by Israel's unfaithfulness, and no one else is being invited to pass judgment.

The note on chapter 28, verses 15 to 46, says how such passages must and must not be used. It applies here.
passages.later:
Jeremiah heard the nations ask the same question about Jerusalem: ‘Why has the LORD done such a thing to this great city?’ (Jeremiah 22:8).

Jeremiah also met the man of verse 19, in people who came to the temple and said, ‘We are delivered, so we can continue with all these abominations’ (Jeremiah 7:10).

The letter to the Hebrews takes up the picture of verse 18 for the church: ‘that no root of bitterness springs up to cause trouble and defile many’ (Hebrews 12:15).
passages.hard:
Verse 20 says that the LORD ‘will never be willing to forgive him’. Can a person put himself beyond forgiveness?

The person in view is described closely. He hears the covenant, says ‘I will have peace’, and goes on in open stubbornness, counting on God to do nothing. He is not sorry and does not mean to be. The verse says that such a stance will not be met with pardon.

It does not describe a person who has done wrong and wants to come back. The very next chapter is addressed to people who have brought the whole curse on themselves, and it promises that when they return, God will have compassion and restore them (30:1-3). The same book that speaks verse 20 says, “you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul” (4:29).

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The man of verse 19 used his membership among God's people as a reason not to change. Ask whether you ever count on belonging to a church, a family or a tradition to cover a way of life you do not intend to give up. And ask what small, hidden root is growing in you now.

passages.t: The secret things and the things revealed
passages.happening: The chapter closes with a single sentence. “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever, so that we may follow all the words of this law” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
After so much warning, the people might be left with hard questions. Why does God give understanding to some and not yet to others? What exactly will happen, and when? How will it all end?

Moses draws a line. There are things God has kept to himself. He calls them ‘the secret things’. They are his, and Israel is not asked to work them out.

And there are ‘the things revealed’. These belong to Israel and to its children. They are given for a purpose, which is to be done. What God has made known is enough to live by.

The verse does not forbid honest questions. It sets an order. A person does not have to solve what is hidden before obeying what is plain.

In the old Hebrew manuscripts the words for ‘to us and to our children’ are marked with unusual dots above the letters. No one is sure what the scribes meant by them.

Coming where it does, the sentence is a mercy. It tells a people who cannot see the future that they have been given what they need.
passages.later:
Through Isaiah God says the same of his own mind: “For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts” (Isaiah 55:9).

Paul, at the end of his hardest chapters, stops explaining and worships: “How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!” (Romans 11:33).

A psalm shows what it is to live at peace with verse 29: ‘I do not aspire to great things or matters too lofty for me’ (Psalm 131:1).
passages.asks: Some things are God's alone, and some have been given to you. Ask which unanswered question you are using as a reason to delay doing what you already know is right. And ask whether you can leave with God what he has not explained, and still trust him with what he has.
